chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-Ala ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
When a man hears testimony and was not called to witness upon it, then he has the choice: if he wishes, he testifies, and if he wishes, he remains silent.

key_terms.الشَّهَادَة: Testimony, legal witness; the formal act of bearing witness in an Islamic legal proceeding
key_terms.بِالْخِيَار: Having free choice, being at liberty; a legal term indicating absence of obligation
key_terms.سَكَتَ: Remained silent; in a legal context, the permissibility of withholding testimony when not formally called

ai.seo_question: Is a person obligated to testify if they heard something but were not called as a witness in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) establishes a key principle in the jurisprudence of testimony: a person who incidentally overhears testimony — without being formally designated as a witness — is under no legal obligation to come forward. This ruling reflects the Islamic principle that testimony carries both a right and a burden, and that the obligation to testify arises only from a formal request. The Imam's teaching was transmitted through a highly reliable chain including Safwan ibn Yahya and Muhammad ibn Muslim, two of the most trusted narrators in early Shia jurisprudence.
